query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Adding trace yttrium to the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA will improve the adhesion of the protective oxide scale during high‐temperature exposure, thereby reducing degradation via scale spallation and delaying catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: An additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an FCC matrix and its as-produced microstructure.
generation.intervention: Introducing a small, controlled amount of trace yttrium (e.g., ~0.5 at.%) into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Exposing samples to elevated temperatures (around 900–1000 °C) in oxidizing atmospheres (and, optionally, reducing gas conditions for comparison).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoscale Y-containing oxide particles (e.g., Y2O3) at the alloy/oxide interface that act as pinning sites.
generation.mechanism: Trace Y ions preferentially segregate to the oxide scale boundary and promote the formation of discrete Y2O3 particulates which enhance oxide-scale adhesion, reduce cation outward diffusion, and mitigate growth stresses. This improved interfacial stability reduces the likelihood of scale spallation, which, if uncontrolled, leads to accelerated degradation and eventual catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy without Y, the Y-modified alloy will exhibit a significantly lower oxidation rate constant, reduced mass loss upon thermal cycling, and enhanced mechanical stability of the oxide scale, thereby delaying or preventing catastrophic failure during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: The performance of the alloy in its original composition (without trace yttrium), which is expected to form an oxide scale that spalls and degrades more rapidly under thermal cycling due to poor interfacial adhesion.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under high-temperature (900–1000 °C) oxidizing conditions; the effect under reducing gases is less certain and possibly less pronounced, so testing across both environments will delineate the boundaries of the mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal concentration of trace Y for maximum benefit, and the degree to which reducing atmosphere exposures might mitigate or alter the yttrium effect, remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA samples: one set with no yttrium (baseline) and one set doped with trace yttrium (~0.5 at.%). Subject both sets to identical high-temperature exposure (900–1000 °C) in an oxidizing environment, with additional tests under reducing conditions as a control. Perform cyclic thermal exposures to simulate prolonged service conditions.
measurements: Mass gain/loss measurements to quantify oxidation rate and scale spallation.
Microscopic analysis (e.g., SEM/TEM) to assess the morphology and adhesion of the oxide scale, specifically checking for the presence of discrete Y2O3 particles.
Mechanical testing (e.g., scratch tests, fracture energy measurements) of the oxide/alloy interface after thermal cycling.
Comparative analysis of oxide-scale thickness and composition via XRD or EDS.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yttrium-doped samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in oxide-scale adhesion, reduced mass change, and lower oxide spallation compared to the baseline samples under oxidizing conditions, or if both Y-doped and undoped samples exhibit similar degradation leading to catastrophic failure, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Beyond conventional alloying, the addition of trace reactive elements, particularly yttrium (Y), has been widely recognized as one of the most effective routes for improving the long-term stability of alumina-forming alloys. This behavior, commonly referred to as the reactive element effect (REE), is generally associated with modified oxide-growth mechanisms, suppressed cation outward diffusion, and enhanced oxide-scale adhesion. According to the dynamic segregation theory [,,], reactive-element ions preferentially segregate to oxide grain boundaries, thereby reducing outward metal-ion diffusion and mitigating growth stress within the scale. In addition, Y-containing oxides may form discrete interfacial anchoring sites, often described as oxide pegs, which mechanically stabilize the scale and inhibit spallation during repeated thermal cycling [,]. Although the REE has been extensively investigated in conventional Ni- and Fe-based superalloys, its interaction with the chemically complex multi-principal-element matrix of HEAs remains insufficiently understood [,]. As shown in Figure 6, the cyclic oxidation results reveal pronounced differences in spallation resistance among the three alloys. The Base Alloy undergoes severe oxide-scale spallation after 100 thermal cycles at 1000 °C, resulting in substantial mass loss. The Synergy Alloy shows improved cyclic oxidation resistance, but measurable scale degradation still occurs. In contrast, the Innovation Alloy exhibits a mass change of only 0.05 ± 0.02 mg/cm2 after 100 cycles, with almost no detectable spallation, demonstrating excellent scale stability under thermal cycling. The simulated stress evolution further indicates that the oxide scale on the Innovation Alloy accumulates growth stress more slowly and can more effectively accommodate stress through local deformation and defect healing. Scratch testing confirms this enhanced interfacial stability: the critical load and interfacial fracture energy reach 78 N and 14.8 J/m2, respectively, which are substantially higher than those of the Synergy Alloy. In summary, this study developed a high-performance FeNiCuAl-based high-entropy alloy coating by revealing a triple-synergy mechanism that integrates Cr-Co-Mn multi-element alloying, trace Y modification, and laser-cladding-induced nanocrystallization. Unlike conventional oxidation-resistant alloy design strategies that mainly rely on complex alloying, this work demonstrates that the rapid solidification effect of laser cladding can generate nanocrystalline grain boundaries, which serve as fast diffusion channels for Al and Cr and promote the rapid formation of a protective MnCr2O4/Al2O3 bilayer scale. The Innovation Alloy (FeNiCuAlCr2.5Co2.5Mn2.5Y0.5) achieved a three-order-of-magnitude reduction in the parabolic oxidation rate constant, reaching 1.7 × 10−6 mg2·cm−4·s−1 at 900 °C, together with excellent scale adhesion, as indicated by a critical load of 78 N. This improvement is closely associated with the nanoscale pinning effect of approximately 35 nm Y2O3 particles at the oxide scale/alloy interface.
